passage:
"Parul, you've read the same page for twenty minutes."
"Didi, I can't breathe properly. Tomorrow's physics paper and I don't remember anything."
"Okay, put the book down. Look at me. Breathe in slowly through your nose."
"This is silly—"
"Humour me. In... now out, even slower, like you're cooling hot tea."
"...Okay."
"Again. Drop your shoulders. They're up near your ears."
"My heart's still going fast."
"That's fine. It'll slow. Now shoes on. We're walking round the building twice."
"Nikita didi, I don't have time!"
"You don't have time to panic either. Ten minutes outside, then back to the book."
Later, climbing the stairs, Parul said, "My head feels less jammed."
"Good. Do that breathing in the exam hall if it starts again. 🙂"

qa.q: How many times did Nikita want to walk round the building?
qa.a: Nikita wanted them to walk round the building twice.

qa.q: What was Parul feeling before Nikita stepped in?
qa.a: Parul was panicking about the physics paper, struggling to breathe properly and sure of remembering nothing.

qa.q: What small step did Nikita suggest for the exam hall itself?
qa.a: She suggested using the same slow breathing if the panic started again during the paper.

qa.q: How does Nikita see Parul's protest about having no time?
qa.a: She sees that panic is wasting more time than a short walk would, so she calmly insists on the break.

grounding: Shows a teen using slow breathing and a brisk walk, coached by Nikita didi, to handle exam anxiety.

passage: Last term I had to present our science project in front of the whole school. The night before, my stomach felt like it was full of wasps. I kept rehearsing in the mirror and getting worse. Afreen called and I told her I might fake a cold. She said, "Jaya, go run. Seriously." So I jogged up and down our lane until my legs burned, then lay on the floor and breathed out long and slow, the way our PE teacher taught us. It didn't magic the fear away, but I slept. Next morning, backstage, my hands went cold again. I pressed my feet into the floor and counted my breaths. My voice shook for the first minute and then it didn't. I finished. People clapped.

qa.q: Who suggested that Jaya go for a run?
qa.a: Afreen did, when she called and said, 'Go run.'

qa.q: What does Jaya's thought of faking a cold show about Jaya's state the night before?
qa.a: Jaya was so anxious that avoiding the presentation felt like the only escape, with a stomach full of wasps and rehearsing only making it worse.

qa.q: Which strategies helped Jaya, and why did they work?
qa.a: Running, slow breathing and pressing her feet into the floor helped because they calmed Jaya's body enough to sleep and to get past the shaky first minute.

qa.q: How might Afreen feel hearing that Jaya finished and people clapped?
qa.a: She would likely feel glad and a bit proud, since her blunt advice helped her friend face the fear instead of hiding. 😊

grounding: A teen recalls handling intense performance anxiety with exercise, breathwork and grounding.

passage:
Coach's note, inter-school chess final, Saturday.

Before round three, Lokesh came to me pale, rubbing his palms on his trousers. He said his mind had gone "blank white" and that his parents had taken the day off to watch. I did not tell him to relax. I asked him to sit, press both feet flat on the floor, and breathe out longer than he breathed in, several times. Then we walked once around the corridor, and I asked him to name five things he could see.

He went back in with steadier hands. He lost the game, but played carefully and did not rush his moves, which is where he usually slips.

Next step: I will practise this routine with the whole team during Tuesday practice, not just before finals. — Jagdish

qa.q: What did Lokesh say had happened to his mind before round three?
qa.a: He said his mind had gone blank white.

qa.q: What might Lokesh have been worried about, based on the note?
qa.a: He seemed afraid of letting his parents down, since they had taken the day off to watch him in the final.

qa.q: Why is the coach's plan to practise the routine on Tuesdays wise?
qa.a: Calming habits work best when they are practised in ordinary moments, so the whole team can reach for them automatically under pressure.

qa.q: What would change if the coach had simply said 'just relax'?
qa.a: Lokesh would probably have felt unheard and stayed tense, because being told to relax gives no concrete way to calm the body.

grounding: A coach records a teen using grounding, slow exhaling and movement to manage competition anxiety.

passage: Thursday, 11 pm. Prelims start Monday, and today in the maths revision test my hands went cold and my brain just stopped. Couldn't even read question 3. Sunaina saw me and did that thing from our PT class: pointed at her own chest and breathed slowly in and out, like a slow balloon. I copied her. Four breaths, maybe five. The numbers came back. Didn't finish, but I did most of it. Tonight I couldn't sleep, so I went up and down our building stairs three times, fast, till my legs burned, and then did the balloon breathing on my bed. Heart's slower now. Writing this down so I remember it works. Maybe I'll ask Sir if we can practise this before Monday. – Kamal

qa.q: What did Sunaina do to help Kamal during the test?
qa.a: She pointed at her chest and breathed slowly in and out.

qa.q: How did Kamal feel when Kamal's hands went cold during the test?
qa.a: Kamal felt panicked and frozen, so anxious that reading the question became impossible.

qa.q: What would you add to Kamal's plan before Monday?
qa.a: Practise the breathing daily while calm so it comes easily in the exam, and tell a teacher or parent if the panic keeps coming.

qa.q: What was it like for Sunaina to see Kamal freeze?
qa.a: Sunaina probably felt worried for Kamal and quickly thought of a quiet way to help without drawing attention. 🙂

grounding: Shows a teenager using slow breathing and physical exercise to calm exam anxiety.

passage: In the small town, the board exams were a week away, and Irawati, sixteen, woke at four with her heart racing. She'd read that breathing slowly helped, so she lay still and counted: in for four, hold for four, out for six. It helped a little. At dawn she laced up her shoes and ran three rounds of the school ground, feet slapping, lungs burning. Her younger brother Jatin found her stretching by the gate. "Running before an exam?" "It empties my head," she said. The next morning he came too. By exam day, she still felt nervous, but it no longer swallowed her.

qa.q: How many rounds of the school ground did Irawati run?
qa.a: Three rounds.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling when she woke at four with her heart racing?
qa.a: She felt anxious and panicky about the upcoming exams.

qa.q: Why are Irawati's breathing and running useful habits?
qa.a: They calm her body so her mind can settle, giving her some control over the anxiety.

qa.q: How might Jatin see his sister's dawn runs?
qa.a: First as strange, then as something worth trying, since he joins her.

grounding: Shows a teenager using breathing and exercise to manage exam anxiety.

passage: The night before her piano recital in Kyoto, Yuki, fifteen, sat on her bed with her hands shaking so badly she couldn't hold a cup. Her friend Jamal, visiting from next door, noticed. "My swimming coach taught me this," he said. "Press your feet flat on the floor. Breathe out longer than you breathe in." Yuki tried it. Five breaths. Ten. Her hands slowed. "Now walk with me round the block." They walked in the cool air, not talking. When she came back, she played the piece once through, softly, and went to sleep. At the recital her hands still trembled a little, but they played.

qa.q: How many breaths did Yuki take before her hands slowed?
qa.a: Ten breaths.

qa.q: What was Yuki feeling when her hands shook?
qa.a: She felt highly anxious and nervous about the recital.

qa.q: What did Jamal's suggestions do well?
qa.a: They gave her simple body-based steps, grounding and slow breathing, then a calm walk.

qa.q: How might Jamal feel seeing Yuki calm down?
qa.a: Relieved and glad his coach's trick worked for his friend.

grounding: Shows a teenager using breathwork and walking to calm performance anxiety with a friend's help.

passage: Before the inter-school debate final, Pema, sixteen, hid in the girls' changing room of the sports complex, breathing fast. Her PE teacher, Sonali Ma'am, found her there. "Talk to me." "I can't breathe properly. My mind's blank." Sonali crouched down. "Shake your hands out, hard. Now roll your shoulders. Good. Breathe in through your nose, slowly, and out through your mouth, like blowing a candle." Pema did it five times. Her shoulders dropped. "Better?" "A bit." "Then walk to the stage with me." Pema stood. Her legs were still wobbly, but she walked.

qa.q: Where did Pema hide before the final?
qa.a: In the girls' changing room of the sports complex.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling when her mind went blank?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed with anxiety and panic before the debate.

qa.q: Which of Sonali Ma'am's steps helped most, and why?
qa.a: Shaking out and slow breathing, because they calmed Pema's body so she could think again.

qa.q: How might Sonali Ma'am feel as Pema walks to the stage?
qa.a: Relieved and proud that Pema used the steps and faced her fear.

grounding: Shows a teenager using physical self-calming strategies, guided by a teacher, to handle anxiety before a debate.

passage:

passage: "The school magazine asked how I handle board stress, so okay. I'm Elizabeth, Class 12. In January I was a mess. I couldn't sleep, my stomach hurt before every mock, I snapped at my mum. Coach Yogesh noticed I'd stopped coming to the track. He said, 'Come back for twenty minutes. Just run.' So I did. Every evening, twenty minutes, even in revision week. Then I added one thing: before each paper, I stand with my feet flat and breathe out longer than I breathe in. Sounds tiny. But my shoulders come down. I still get nervous. The difference is now I know what to do with it. And I sleep."

qa.q: How long does Elizabeth run each evening?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth feel in January?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt anxious and on edge, unable to sleep, with stomach aches and snapping at home.

qa.q: What routine did Elizabeth build to manage her stress?
qa.a: Running for twenty minutes each evening and breathing out longer than breathing in before each paper.

qa.q: How might Coach Yogesh feel seeing Elizabeth back on the track?
qa.a: He would likely feel relieved and glad his suggestion helped Elizabeth.

grounding: A teenager describes using running and slow breathing to manage exam stress.

passage: I'm Zeenat, and I sat behind Ojas in the exam hall on Monday. Before the paper came, I saw his leg jiggling so fast the bench shook. His face was pale. Then he did something odd. He put both feet flat on the floor, pressed his palms together hard, and breathed out slowly, like blowing through a straw. Four or five times. Then he rolled his shoulders back. His leg stopped. When the paper came, he read it without rushing. Afterwards I asked him about it. He said the school counsellor taught him, and that it doesn't make the fear disappear, just smaller. I don't know how he really felt inside, but he looked calm enough to write.

qa.q: What did Ojas do with his palms?
qa.a: He pressed them together hard.

qa.q: What might Ojas have been feeling before the paper came?
qa.a: He was probably very anxious, with his leg jiggling and his face pale.

qa.q: What could other students learn from Ojas's routine?
qa.a: That simple body steps, like planting the feet and slow out-breaths, can help calm nerves before an exam.

qa.q: How does Zeenat see Ojas's routine?
qa.a: Zeenat first finds it odd, then becomes curious and a little impressed, though unsure how he felt inside.

passage:
Monday: Lalit froze during the class presentation practice. His mouth went dry and his heart pounded so hard he couldn't hear his own words. He sat down halfway through, burning.
Wednesday: His friend Jaya, who did kabaddi, showed him what her coach taught before matches: breathe in for four counts, hold, breathe out slowly for longer. "And shake your hands out first. Looks silly, works." Lalit practised in the corridor, feeling foolish. He also went for a run that evening, which he hadn't done in months.
The next Monday: before his turn, Lalit shook out his hands under the desk and did five slow breaths. His voice wobbled at the start, then steadied. He finished. Jaya gave a small thumbs up from the back row.

qa.q: How did Lalit feel during the first presentation practice?

passage:
Sharmila, you're worried about your board exams, I can see it. Let me tell you about me at your age.
I, Hafsa, was the girl who couldn't sleep before any test. The night before my Class 10 exams, my heart raced so hard I thought something was wrong with me. My elder sister found me pacing the roof at midnight.
She didn't tell me to stop being silly. She walked with me, round and round the water tank, and made me count my steps out loud. Then we lay on the mat and she said, breathe in with the stars, out with the street lights. Silly, but I slept.
After that, before every exam, I walked and counted. I still do it before hard meetings.
So come, walk with me tonight.

qa.q: Where did Hafsa's sister find Hafsa at midnight?
qa.a: Pacing the roof.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling the night before the Class 10 exams?
qa.a: Hafsa felt very anxious and frightened, with a racing heart that made her think something was wrong.

qa.q: What was the turning point inside Hafsa's story?
qa.a: Her sister walking with her and making her count steps and breathe, which gave Hafsa a way to calm herself that she still uses.

qa.q: How might the elder sister have felt finding Hafsa on the roof?
qa.a: She may have felt worried but calm enough to stay and help instead of scolding.

grounding: An elder recalls learning as a teen to use walking and breathing to ease exam anxiety.

passage:
The school bus broke down on the highway, and Santosh's chemistry practical started in forty minutes. He had revised all night. Now he was stuck on a hot roadside with twenty kids and a driver on the phone.
His hands started to shake. He felt his breath go short and fast.
Nitin, next to him, said, "Do the thing from PE."
Santosh closed his eyes. Feet flat. Breathe in, slow count, breathe out longer. He pressed his palms together hard, then let go. Again. Again.
The replacement bus came twenty minutes later. He reached the lab late but the teacher let him start.
His hands were still a bit unsteady on the burette. But his mind was clear enough to read the scale.

qa.q: How long before the practical did the bus break down?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Santosh feeling on the roadside?
qa.a: He felt panicked and anxious; his hands shook and his breath went short and fast.

qa.q: What helped Santosh most, and why?
qa.a: Slow breathing and pressing his palms together calmed his body enough that his mind stayed clear for the practical.

qa.q: What is it like for Nitin to watch Santosh panic?
qa.a: Nitin seems concerned but steady, and his reminder helps Santosh remember what to do.

grounding: Shows a teen using breath and body techniques to steady himself under academic pressure.

passage: Outside the board exam hall in Lucknow, students crowded the corridor, flipping through notes. Imran's hands were cold and his heart was thudding so hard he could hear it. The words on his notes wouldn't stay still. His friend Madhuri noticed him gripping the railing. "Do the thing," she said. Imran closed his notes and pressed his feet flat on the floor. He breathed in slowly through his nose, held it, and let it out even more slowly, the way he'd practised all month after his evening runs. Four rounds. His shoulders came down from his ears. The bell rang. He rolled his neck once, nodded at Madhuri and walked in, notes left in his bag.

qa.q: What was Imran gripping when Madhuri noticed him?
qa.a: He was gripping the railing.

qa.q: How was Imran feeling in the corridor before the breathing?
qa.a: He was very anxious, with cold hands and a thudding heart, and couldn't focus on his notes.

qa.q: Why did Imran's breathing work in that moment?
qa.a: He had practised it all month after his runs, so in the corridor it was familiar and his body calmed quickly. 👍

qa.q: What is it like for Madhuri to see Imran so tense?
qa.a: Madhuri is concerned but calm, and knows a short reminder, "Do the thing", is enough to help.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager using practised slow breathing and grounding to calm exam anxiety.
